Pharaoh's dreams (verses 1–8)

Pharaoh's dreams became the means by which Joseph was released from prison.

Henry says that, since God no longer speaks to us in this way, we need not pay much attention to our dreams or be eager to tell them. Recounting foolish dreams can produce little more than foolish conversation.

But these particular dreams were clearly sent by God: Pharaoh awoke deeply troubled.

Joseph interprets Pharaoh's dreams (verses 9–32)

God's time to deliver his people is always the most suitable time.

If the chief cupbearer had arranged Joseph's release earlier, Joseph would probably have returned to the land of the Hebrews.

Then he would not have received such blessing himself, or become such a blessing to his family.

When Joseph was brought before Pharaoh, he gave God the honor.

Pharaoh had dreamed that he was standing beside the Nile and saw both fat and thin cows emerging from it.

Henry observes that Egypt's plenty depends on the Nile's overflow rather than on rainfall.

See how many different ways Providence distributes its gifts! Yet our dependence remains on the same First Cause, who makes every creature—rain or river—what it is to us.

See how changeable the comforts of this life are. We cannot be certain that tomorrow will resemble today, or next year this one.

We must learn both how to live with little and how to live with abundance.

Notice God's goodness in sending seven years of plenty before seven years of famine, so that provisions could be stored.

The earth produces more in some seasons and less in others. Yet when all is considered together, those who gather much have nothing left over, and those who gather little lack nothing (Exodus 16:18).

Notice, too, how quickly worldly pleasures and possessions pass away.

The enormous harvests of the good years were swallowed up by the famine years. What seemed so plentiful was barely sufficient to keep the people alive.

But there is bread that lasts to eternal life. That is the bread worth working for.

Those who make earthly things their highest good will find little satisfaction in remembering that they once enjoyed them.

Joseph advises Pharaoh and is raised to power (verses 33–45)

Joseph gave Pharaoh wise counsel. A clear warning should be followed by good advice.

God has warned us in his word of a coming day of trial, when we will need all the grace we can receive.

We should therefore make provision now.

Pharaoh spoke honorably of Joseph, recognizing him as a man in whom God's Spirit was present. Such people deserve to be valued.

Pharaoh gave Joseph the marks of high rank and a name expressing the value he placed on him: Zaphnath-paaneah, which Henry explains as “revealer of secrets.”

Some have interpreted the name instead as “savior of the world.” Henry presents that as another proposed translation, not as the only possible meaning.

Joseph's advancement encourages everyone to trust God.

But all the brightest glory, even the glory of heaven, belongs to Christ.

God has entrusted the highest office to his hands and given him all authority in heaven and on earth.

Joseph prepares for the famine (verses 46–57)

In naming his sons Manasseh and Ephraim, Joseph acknowledged God's providence.

First, God made him forget his suffering. Second, God made him fruitful in the land where he had been afflicted.

The seven years of plenty came—and then they ended.

We should remember that both our times of prosperity and our opportunities to do good will come to an end.

We must not become complacent when life goes well or lazy about using our opportunities.

The good years will end. Whatever your hand finds to do, do it. Gather while there is time to gather.

Then the shortage came, and famine spread beyond Egypt into other lands.

Joseph had been diligent in storing food during the years of plenty. When famine arrived, he was prudent and careful in distributing it.

He was occupied with important and useful work.

Yet while he was doing all this, his father Jacob was saying, “Joseph is no more!”

How much trouble would vanish if only we knew the whole truth.

These events should turn our thoughts to Jesus.

Throughout the world there is a famine of the bread of life.

Go to Jesus and do whatever he tells you. Listen to his voice and come to him.

He will open his treasures and satisfy hungry souls in every age and nation, without money and without price.

But those who reject this provision must starve; his enemies will be destroyed.

Jacob sends his sons to Egypt (verses 1–6)

Jacob saw that his neighbors had bought grain in Egypt and brought it home. Seeing others receive what they need can spur us to act.

Will other people find food for their souls while we starve, even though that food is available?

Once we know where help can be found, we should seek it promptly, without shrinking from the effort or resenting the expense.

This is especially true when our immortal souls are at stake.

Christ has made provision for us, but we must come to him and seek it from him.

Joseph deals sternly with his brothers (verses 7–20)

Joseph treated his brothers harshly, not to take revenge but to lead them to repentance.

When he did not see Benjamin with them, he suspected they might have disposed of him as they had disposed of Joseph.

He therefore gave them opportunities to speak about their father and brother.

In his providence, God sometimes seems harsh toward those he loves and speaks sternly to people for whom he has great mercy in store.

Joseph finally decided that one of the brothers would remain behind while the others returned home to bring Benjamin.

His statement, “I fear God,” should have encouraged them.

It was as though he said, “You can trust me not to wrong you. I dare not do so, because I know that someone greater than I am stands over me.”

We can expect fair treatment from those who truly fear God.

The brothers remember their guilt (verses 21–24)

One task of conscience is to bring back to mind things said and done long ago.

When Joseph's brothers first committed their crime, they treated it lightly and sat down to eat.

But now, many years later, their consciences accused them.

This shows one benefit of suffering: it can awaken conscience and bring forgotten sins back to our attention.

It also shows the burden of guilt for wrongs done to others.

When we think someone has wronged us, we ought to remember how we ourselves have wronged other people.

Reuben alone could look back with some comfort. He had done what he could to prevent the crime.

When others suffer, it is a great comfort to know that we did not join in their wrongdoing but spoke against it as best we could.

Joseph withdrew and wept.

His judgment told him to continue treating his brothers as strangers because they were not yet humbled enough.

But his natural love for them still moved him deeply.

The brothers return with grain and money (verses 25–28)

The brothers came seeking grain, and grain they received.

More than that, each found that his money had been returned.

Christ, like Joseph, provides what we need without money and without price. Even the poorest are invited to come and receive.

But a guilty conscience often interprets God's kindness as a threat.

People burdened by guilt may read evil meanings into events that are actually working for their good.

Jacob refuses to send Benjamin (verses 29–38)

Jacob was deeply troubled by the report his sons brought home.

Even the money Joseph had kindly returned frightened him.

He blamed his sons, fearing that they had provoked the Egyptians and had wrongfully taken back the money.

Jacob plainly distrusted them. He remembered that he had never seen Joseph again after Joseph went away with them.

A family is in a sad state when children behave so badly that their parents no longer know whether they can trust them.

Jacob regarded Joseph as lost and Simeon and Benjamin as endangered.

“All these things are against me,” he concluded.

But it turned out that all of them were working for his good and the good of his family.

We often think that something is against us when it is actually working in our favor.

We suffer in our health, possessions, reputation, and relationships and suppose that everything is against us.

Yet those very troubles can be working for us an eternal weight of glory.

So the Lord Jesus sometimes hides himself and his favor, correcting people for whom he has loving purposes.

Through painful correction and humbling conviction, he breaks the stubbornness and pride of the heart and brings people to true repentance.

Even before sinners fully know him or experience his grace, he seeks their good and sustains them as they wait for him.

May we do the same: refuse discouragement, look for no other refuge, and humble ourselves more and more under his mighty hand.

At the right time, he will answer our prayers and do more for us than we expect.

Jacob agrees to send Benjamin (verses 1–14)

Jacob urged his sons to go and buy a little more food. In a time of shortage, even a little must be enough.

Judah insisted that Benjamin must go with them.

Children do not dishonor their parents or neglect their duty when they humbly offer advice and, when necessary, reason with them.

Jacob saw that there was no alternative and agreed.

His prudence and fairness appeared in three decisions.

First, he sent back the money found in their sacks.

Honesty requires us to return not only what we obtained through our own fault but also what reached us through someone else's mistake.

Even when something comes to us by an oversight, keeping it after discovering the error is dishonest.

Second, Jacob sent twice as much money as before. Grain prices might have risen, or they might have to pay a ransom for Simeon.

Third, he sent a gift of products available in Canaan but scarce in Egypt, including balm and honey.

Providence does not distribute the same gifts everywhere.

Yet honey and spices cannot replace grain for bread.

Canaan was suffering from severe famine, but it still had balm, myrrh, and similar goods.

We can live adequately on plain food without delicacies, but we cannot live on delicacies without ordinary food.

Let us thank God that what we most need and find most useful is generally the most common and affordable.

People prize gold, silver, and the luxury products of each country.

But in a famine they readily exchange them for bread.

How little use will earthly treasures be on the day of wrath!

How readily we should count them all as loss for the surpassing worth of knowing Jesus Christ.

If we wish to prevail with people, we should first prevail with God in earnest prayer.

Yet every request for the blessings of this life, and every request to be spared its sufferings, should end with “Your will be done.”

Joseph receives his brothers; they are afraid (verses 15–25)

Jacob's sons returned to Egypt for a second time to buy grain.

If we ever experience a famine of God's word, we should not complain about having to travel as far for spiritual food as these men did for physical food.

Joseph had instructed his steward to bring them into his house.

Even this frightened them. Those who are burdened by guilt tend to interpret everything in the worst possible light.

But the steward reassured them.

His words suggest that Joseph, a good master, had introduced him to the knowledge of the true God, the God of the Hebrews.

Faithful servants should take suitable opportunities to speak seriously and reverently about God and his providence.

Joseph prepares a feast for his brothers (verses 26–34)

Notice the deep respect Joseph's brothers showed him. In this way his dreams were increasingly fulfilled.

Joseph treated them with great kindness and generosity.

But notice also how early the distinction between Jews and Gentiles appears in this account.

In a famine, receiving enough food would have been a great blessing. Instead, they were given a feast.

Their worries and fears were now gone. They ate joyfully, believing that they were at peace with the ruler of the land.

If God accepts our work and what we bring before him, we have reason to rejoice.

Joseph showed special favor to Benjamin, testing whether his brothers would envy him.

We should be content with what we have and not resent what others possess.

Likewise, Jesus increasingly shows those he loves how much they need him.

He teaches them that he is their only refuge from destruction, overcomes their reluctance, and brings them to himself.

Then, when he sees fit, he lets them taste his love and welcomes them to the provision of his house as a foretaste of the greater blessings he intends for them.

But, Thy will be done, should close every petition for the mercies of this life, or against the afflictions of this life.

Verses 15-25
Jacob's sons went down the second time into Egypt to buy corn. If we should ever know what a famine of the word means, let us not think it much to travel as far for spiritual food, as they did for bodily food. Joseph's steward had orders from his master to take them to his house. Even this frightened them. Those that are guilty make the worst of every thing. But the steward encouraged them. It appears, from what he said, that by his good master he was brought to the knowledge of the true God, the God of the Hebrews. Religious servants should take all fit occasions to speak of God and his providence, with reverence and seriousness.

He makes them see that he is their only refuge from destruction. He overcomes their unwillingness, and brings them to himself. Then, as he sees good, he gives them some taste of his love, and welcomes them to the provisions of his house, as an earnest of what he further intends for them.

Joseph tests his brothers' love for Benjamin (verses 1–17)

Joseph wanted to discover how his brothers now felt about Benjamin.

If they still envied and hated Rachel's other son as they had hated Joseph, or if they still showed the same lack of concern for their father Jacob, their behavior would now reveal it.

When the cup was found in Benjamin's sack, they had an excuse to leave him behind as a slave.

But we cannot judge what people are now only by what they used to be, or predict what they will do simply by what they have done.

Joseph's steward accused them of ingratitude: they were repaying kindness with wrongdoing.

He also accused them of foolishness. Why steal a cup used every day, which would quickly be missed and carefully sought?

Henry explains that the steward's accusation can be understood in two ways.

Joseph might have had a particular attachment to the cup, so that he would search thoroughly for it if it disappeared.

Or Joseph might have left it at their table deliberately to see whether they were honest.

The brothers placed themselves at Joseph's mercy and acknowledged that God's judgment was righteous.

Perhaps they were thinking of their old wrong against Joseph and believed that God was now calling them to account for it.

Even when people wrong us and we suffer unjustly at their hands, we must still acknowledge that God is righteous and that he brings our sins to light.

Judah pleads for Benjamin (verses 18–34)

Even if Joseph had been a complete stranger to the family, as Judah supposed, Judah's powerful appeal could hardly have failed to move him.

But neither Jacob nor Benjamin needed an intercessor to persuade Joseph to love them. He already loved them.

Judah now remained faithfully at Benjamin's side in his distress.

Much later, that loyalty was repaid when the tribe of Benjamin remained with the tribe of Judah after the other tribes had abandoned it.

When the apostle discusses Christ's mediation, he notes that our Lord descended from Judah (Hebrews 7:14).

Christ not only interceded for transgressors; he became their Surety, showing tender concern for both his Father and his brothers and sisters.

Jesus, the great fulfillment of what Joseph foreshadows, humbles and tests his people even after they have enjoyed some of his kindness.

He brings their sins back to mind so that they may truly repent, show their repentance, and recognize how much they owe to his mercy.

He brings their sins to their remembrance, that they may exercise and show repentance, and feel how much they owe to his mercy.

Simeon and Levi were hot-tempered and revengeful.

Their murder of the Shechemites revealed their character, and Jacob condemned that barbaric act.

Our souls are our honor. Their powers distinguish us from the animals that perish and raise us above them.

We should sincerely detest people who delight in bloodshed and harm.

“Cursed be their anger.”

Jacob cursed not their persons, but their sinful passions.

“I will divide them.”

For Levi, that judgment was later turned into a blessing.

The Levites served God acceptably when they acted with zeal against those worshiping the golden calf (Exodus 32).

God set them apart for the priesthood, and in that role they were scattered among the people of Israel.

Judah and the promised Messiah (verses 8–12)

The name Judah means “praise.”

God was praised when Judah was born (Genesis 29:35), praised by him, and praised in him.

It was fitting that his brothers should praise him.

Judah would become a strong and courageous tribe.

He was pictured not as a lion roaming furiously and causing distress, but as one resting peacefully in the satisfaction of his power and success.

That is a picture of true greatness.

Judah would become the royal tribe, the line from which the Messiah, the Prince, would come.

Shiloh, the promised Seed through whom the earth would be blessed, would come from Judah.

Henry gives the name the sense of “the peaceful and prosperous One” or “Savior.”

From far away in history, the dying Jacob saw the day of Christ.

That hope comforted and sustained him on his deathbed.

Judah retained authority until Christ's coming.

After Christ's crucifixion, according to Henry, that authority was diminished. As Jesus had foretold, Jerusalem was destroyed, and the remaining Jewish people, scattered and afflicted, were mingled together.

Much of the blessing pronounced over Judah applies to our Lord Jesus.

Christ has an abundance of everything that nourishes and refreshes the soul, sustains spiritual life, and fills it with joy.

He is the true Vine.

Wine is the appointed symbol of his blood: blood shed for sinners, received through faith, and truly life-giving.

All the blessings of the gospel are offered like wine and milk, without money or payment.

Every thirsty soul is welcome (Isaiah 55:1).

Zebulun, Issachar, and Dan (verses 13–18)

If prophecy declares that Zebulun will become a haven for ships, we may be certain that Providence will place his people there.

God determines the boundaries of the places where we live.

It is our wisdom and duty to accept our circumstances and make good use of them.

If Zebulun lives near the sea, let him make that shore a haven for ships.

Issachar saw that the land was pleasant.

It offered both beautiful views and fruitful harvests to reward his labor.

With the eyes of faith, let us see how good the rest of heaven is and how delightful that promised land will be.

That hope makes our present duties easier.

Dan would gain advantage over his enemies through skill, strategy, and surprise, like a serpent striking a traveler's heel.

Jacob was almost spent and near fainting.

He refreshed himself with the words, “I have waited for your salvation, O Lord!”

The salvation he awaited was Christ, the promised Seed.

As Jacob prepared to be gathered to his people, he longed for the One to whom the people would be gathered.

He openly confessed that he sought heaven, the better country (Hebrews 11:13–14).

Now he was about to enjoy that salvation, and it comforted him to know that he had waited for it.

We must wait upon Christ as our way to heaven, and wait for heaven as our rest in Christ.

For a dying believer, it is a deep comfort to have waited for the Lord's salvation, because at last he will receive what he has been waiting for.

Gad, Asher, and Naphtali (verses 19–21)

In speaking of Gad, Jacob alluded to his name, which means “troop,” and foretold the character of his tribe.

God's cause and God's people may for a time seem beaten down and defeated, but they will finally be victorious.

This is also a picture of the Christian's struggle.

The grace at work in the soul may seem to lose its battles when bands of sinful desires overcome it.

But the cause belongs to God.

In the end, grace will prevail, making the believer more than a conqueror (Romans 8:37).

Asher would become a prosperous tribe.

His inheritance bordered on Carmel, a place proverbial for its fruitfulness.

Naphtali is described as a deer set free.

Henry takes this as a description of the tribe's character.

Unlike the hard-working ox or donkey, it would prize freedom and ease.

It would be lively and quick to act, though less distinguished by steady, persistent labor.

It would also resemble a petitioner who uses gracious words to ask for mercy.

People with different temperaments and gifts should not criticize or envy one another.

Joseph and Benjamin (verses 22–27)

Jacob's blessing upon Joseph was especially rich.

What he said was both a history of Joseph's past and a prophecy of what would come.

Jacob recalled the many hardships and fiery arrows of temptation Joseph had endured.

Through those trials, Joseph's faith had not failed.

He carried his burdens steadily and did nothing unworthy of his calling.

All the strength we have to resist temptation and bear suffering comes from God.

His grace is enough.

Joseph became the shepherd of Israel, caring for his father and family.

He was also the stone of Israel, the foundation and strong support on which they depended.

In these ways Joseph foreshadowed the Good Shepherd and the tested Cornerstone of God's whole church.

The blessings promised to Joseph's descendants pointed toward the vast and everlasting blessings given to Christ's spiritual offspring.

Jacob blessed all his sons, but Joseph especially, calling him the one “separated from his brothers.”

That separation meant more than his years in Egypt.

He had also been raised to exceptional honor and had shown unusual devotion to God.

Of Benjamin Jacob said, “He shall devour like a wolf.”

The words came through the Spirit of prophecy, not through Jacob's natural preferences.

Otherwise he would have spoken more tenderly of Benjamin, whom he loved so dearly.

Instead, he foretold that Benjamin's descendants would become a warlike people—strong, bold, active, and enriched by the spoils of their enemies.

The apostle Paul belonged to this tribe (Romans 11:1; Philippians 3:5).

Early in life he attacked like a wolf, devouring prey as a persecutor.

Later he distributed the spoils as a preacher of the gospel.

In doing so, he shared in the victory of the Lion of Judah and helped to advance his triumphs.

Jacob gives his final instructions and dies (verses 28–33)

Jacob blessed each son according to the blessings God intended eventually to give his descendants.

He instructed them about his burial place because he believed God's promise that Canaan would one day belong to his offspring.

When he had finished speaking his blessings and instructions, his testimony was complete.

He then prepared for the work of dying.

He drew his feet up into the bed.

This was not only a sign of patient submission to death, but also of someone gladly settling down to rest after a long and weary life.

He freely entrusted his spirit to God, the Father of spirits.

If God's people are our people, death will gather us to them.

Under the care of Israel's Shepherd, we will lack nothing necessary for body or soul.

We will remain here until our work is finished.

Then, breathing our souls into the hands of the One whose salvation we have awaited, we will depart in peace and leave a blessing to our children.

Verses 1-2
All Jacob's sons were living. His calling them together was a precept for them to unite in love, not to mingle with the Egyptians; and foretold that they should not be separated, as Abraham's sons and Isaac's were, but should all make one people. We are not to consider this address as the expression of private feelings of affection, resentment, or partiality; but as the language of the Holy Ghost, declaring the purpose of God respecting the character, circumstances, and situation of the tribes which descended from the sons of Jacob, and which may be traced in their histories.
[Gen.49.3-Gen.49.7]
Verses 3-7
Reuben was the first-born; but by gross sin, he forfeited the birthright. The character of Reuben is, that he was unstable as water. Men do not thrive, because they do not fix. Reuben's sin left a lasting infamy upon his family. Let us never do evil, then we need not fear being told of it. Simeon and Levi were passionate and revengeful. The murder of the Shechemites is a proof of this. Jacob protested against that barbarous act. Our soul is our honour; by its powers we are distinguished from, and raised above, the beasts that perish. We ought, from our hearts, to abhor all bloody and mischievous men. Cursed be their anger. Jacob does not curse their persons, but their lusts. I will divide them. The sentence as it respects Levi was turned into a blessing. This tribe performed an acceptable service in their zeal against the worshippers of the golden calf, Ex 32. Being set apart to God as priests, they were in that character scattered through the nation of Israel.
[Gen.49.8-Gen.49.12]
Verses 8-12
Judah's name signifies praise. God was praised for him, chap. 29:35, praised by him, and praised in him; therefore his brethren shall praise him. Judah should be a strong and courageous tribe. Judah is compared, not to a lion raging and ranging, but to a lion enjoying the satisfaction of his power and success, without creating vexation to others; this is to be truly great. Judah should be the royal tribe, the tribe from which Messiah the Prince should come. Shiloh, that promised Seed in whom the earth should be blessed, "that peaceable and prosperous One," or "Saviour," he shall come of Judah. Thus dying Jacob at a great distance saw Christ's day, and it was his comfort and support on his death-bed. Till Christ's coming, Judah possessed authority, but after his crucifixion this was shortened, and according to what Christ foretold, Jerusalem was destroyed, and all the poor harassed remnant of Jews were confounded together. Much which is here said concerning Judah, is to be applied to our Lord Jesus. In him there is plenty of all which is nourishing and refreshing to the soul, and which maintains and cheers the Divine life in it. He is the true Vine; wine is the appointed symbol of his blood, which is drink indeed, as shed for sinners, and applied in faith; and all the blessings of his gospel are wine and milk, without money and without price, to which every thirsty soul is welcome. [Isa.55.1] Is 55:1.
[Gen.49.13-Gen.49.18]
Verses 13-18
Concerning Zebulun: if prophecy says, Zebulun shall be a haven of ships, be sure Providence will so plant him. God appoints the bounds of our habitation. It is our wisdom and duty to accommodate ourselves to our lot, and to improve it; if Zebulun dwell at the heaven of the sea, let him be for a haven of ships. Concerning Issachar: he saw that the land was pleasant, yielding not only pleasant prospects, but pleasant fruits to recompense his toils. Let us, with an eye of faith, see the heavenly rest to be good, and that land of promise to be pleasant; this will make our present services easy. Dan should, by art, and policy, and surprise, gain advantages against his enemies, like a serpent biting the heel of the traveller. Jacob, almost spent, and ready to faint, relieves himself with those words, "I have waited for thy salvation, O Lord!" The salvation he waited for was Christ, the promised Seed; now that he was going to be gathered to his people, he breathes after Him to whom the gathering of the people shall be. He declared plainly that he sought heaven, the better country, [Heb.11.13] He 11:13, [Heb.11.14] 14. Now he is going to enjoy the salvation, he comforts himself that he had waited for the salvation. Christ, as our way to heaven, is to be waited on; and heaven, as our rest in Christ, is to be waited for. It is the comfort of a dying saint thus to have waited for the salvation of the Lord; for then he shall have what he has been waiting for.
[Gen.49.19-Gen.49.21]
Verses 19-21
Concerning Gad, Jacob alludes to his name, which signifies a troop, and foresees the character of that tribe. The cause of God and his people, though for a time it may seem to be baffled and run down, will be victorious at last. It represents the Christian's conflict. Grace in the soul is often foiled in its conflicts; troops of corruption overcome it, but the cause is God's, and grace will in the end come off conqueror, yea, more than conqueror, [Rom.8.37] Ro 8:37. Asher should be a rich tribe. His inheritance bordered upon Carmel, which was fruitful to a proverb. Naphtali, is a hind let loose. We may consider it as a description of the character of this tribe. Unlike the laborious ox and ass; desirous of ease and liberty; active, but more noted for quick despatch than steady labour and perseverance. Like the suppliant who, with goodly words, craves mercy. Let not those of different tempers and gifts censure or envy one another.
[Gen.49.22-Gen.49.27]
Verses 22-27
The blessing of Joseph is very full. What Jacob says of him, is history as well as prophecy. Jacob reminds him of the difficulties and fiery darts of temptations he had formerly struggled through. His faith did not fail, but through his trials he bore all his burdens with firmness, and did not do anything unbecoming. All our strength for resisting temptations, and bearing afflictions, comes from God; his grace is sufficient. Joseph became the shepherd of Israel, to take care of his father and family; also the stone of Israel, their foundation and strong support. In this, as in many other things, Joseph was a remarkable type of the Good Shepherd, and tried Corner Stone of the whole church of God. Blessings are promised to Joseph's posterity, typical of the vast and everlasting blessings which come upon the spiritual seed of Christ. Jacob blessed all his sons, but especially Joseph, "who was separated from his brethren." Not only separated in Egypt, but, possessing eminent dignity, and more devoted to God. Of Benjamin it is said, He shall ravin as a wolf. Jacob was guided in what he said by the Spirit of prophecy, and not by natural affection; else he would have spoken with more tenderness of his beloved son Benjamin. Concerning him he only foresees and foretells, that his posterity should be a warlike tribe, strong and daring, and that they should enrich themselves with the spoils of their enemies; that they should be active. Blessed Paul was of this tribe, [Rom.11.1] Ro 11:1; [Phil.3.5] Php 3:5; he, in the morning of his day, devoured the prey as a persecutor, but in the evening divided the spoils as a preacher; he shared the blessings of Judah's Lion, and assisted in his victories.
[Gen.49.28-Gen.49.33]
Verses 28-33
Jacob blessed every one according to the blessings God in after-times intended to bestow upon them. He spoke about his burial-place, from a principle of faith in the promise of God, that Canaan should be the inheritance of his seed in due time. When he had finished both his blessing and his charge, and so had finished his testimony, he addressed himself to his dying work. He gathered up his feet into the bed, not only as one patiently submitting to the stroke, but as one cheerfully composing himself to rest, now that he was weary. He freely gave up his spirit into the hand of God, the Father of spirits. If God's people be our people, death will gather us to them. Under the care of the Shepherd of Israel, we shall lack nothing for body or soul. We shall remain unmoved until our work is finished; then, breathing out our souls into His hands for whose salvation we have waited, we shall depart in peace, and leave a blessing for our children after us.

Joseph mourns his father (verses 1–6)

When godly relatives or friends die, we may grieve our loss even if they lived to a good old age and we are confident they have gone to glory.

It is right to honor their memory by mourning them.

Grace does not destroy natural affection.

Instead, it purifies, moderates, and directs it.

We can no longer show tokens of affection to the departed soul.

Yet it is fitting to honor the body, from which we hope for a glorious and joyful resurrection, whatever may happen to its remains in this world.

Joseph showed both faith in God and love for his father.

He ordered Jacob's body to be embalmed, or preserved by wrapping it with spices.

Notice how frail and lowly our bodies become once the soul has departed.

Without preservation, they quickly decay and become offensive.

Jacob is buried (verses 7–14)

Jacob's body was accompanied not only by his family, but also by the leading people of Egypt.

As the Egyptians came to know the Hebrews better, they began to respect them.

Those who profess faith should seek, through wisdom and love, to overcome other people's prejudices against them.

Onlookers recognized how deeply everyone mourned.

The death of godly people is a loss to any place, and it deserves sincere lament.

Joseph forgives and reassures his brothers (verses 15–21)

Many reasons may have led Jacob's sons to remain in Egypt, despite Abraham's prophetic vision that his descendants would one day suffer bondage there.

Judging Joseph by the usual tendencies of human nature, they feared that he would now avenge himself on those who had hated and injured him without reason.

They could neither resist him nor run away.

So they sought to soften his heart by humbling themselves.

They pleaded as servants of the God whom Jacob had worshiped.

Joseph was deeply moved to see his dreams so completely fulfilled.

He told them not to fear him, but to fear God—to humble themselves before the Lord and seek his forgiveness.

He assured them that he himself would continue to treat them kindly.

What an excellent spirit Joseph showed!

Let us learn from him to repay evil with good.

He comforted his brothers and spoke tenderly to them, removing their fears.

People whose spirits have been broken need to be supported and encouraged.

If we love and forgive people, we must not only do good to them. We should speak kindly to them as well.

Joseph gives instructions about his bones and dies (verses 22–26)

Joseph had honored his father, and his days were long in the land God had given him for the time being.

When he knew his own death was approaching, he comforted his brothers with God's promise that their people would return to Canaan in due time.

We should comfort others with the comfort God has given us and encourage them to depend on the promises that sustain us.

To declare his own faith and strengthen theirs, Joseph instructed them not to bury his remains permanently until the great day when his people would settle in the promised land.

By faith in the resurrection and in God's promise of Canaan, Joseph gave instructions concerning his bones.

Those instructions would help keep alive the expectation of their departure from Egypt.

They would constantly turn the people's thoughts toward Canaan and keep Joseph's descendants closely bound to their brothers.

Joseph's death, like his life, showed the excellence of his faith.

Both encourage us to persevere in serving God.

How blessed it is to begin the race toward heaven early, continue steadfastly, and finish the course with joy.

Joseph did so, and by God's grace we may do the same.

Even when death's pains come, if we have trusted the One in whom the patriarchs, prophets, and apostles trusted, we need not fear to say:

“My flesh and my heart may fail, but God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever.”
